description: Test your knowledge of PA G6 | Infections, Genetic & Environmental Disease. Focus on host-pathogen interactions, malaria pathogenesis, and parasitic infections.

cards.text: What is the difference between pathogenicity and virulence?
cards.answer: Pathogenicity is the ability of an organism to cause disease; virulence is the degree/severity of that ability, determined by toxin production, adhesion molecules, capsule, and intracellular survival mechanisms.

tip.tip: Pathogenicity = Can it cause disease? | Virulence = How severe is it?

cards.text: Name the tissue reaction pattern and pathogen class: a suppurative abscess with neutrophilic infiltrate.
cards.answer: Pyogenic bacteria cause suppurative (neutrophilic) inflammation with abscess formation.

tip.tip: Pus (suppuration) = Pyogenic bacteria; think Staph/Strep abscesses

cards.text: What is the hepatic stage of Plasmodium life cycle called, and why is it clinically silent?
cards.answer: Hepatic schizogony occurs in liver hepatocytes. It is clinically silent because no parasites are in the bloodstream; P. vivax/ovale also form dormant hypnozoites here.

tip.tip: Liver = Silent stage (no blood parasites = no symptoms yet)

cards.text: What does PfEMP1 do and why is it critical to P. falciparum pathogenesis?
cards.answer: PfEMP1 (P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1) is expressed on infected RBC knobs, binds endothelial receptors (ICAM-1, CD36), and causes cytoadherence/sequestration in deep microvasculature—preventing splenic destruction.

cards.text: What are Dürck's granulomas and in which form of malaria are they pathognomonic?
cards.answer: Dürck's granulomas are microglial nodules surrounding necrotic vessels in cerebral capillaries; they are pathognomonic of cerebral malaria caused by P. falciparum sequestration.

tip.tip: Dürck = Dead vessels (necrotic) defended by Microglia; seen in Brain malaria

cards.text: What is malarial pigment (haemozoin) and where is it most abundant?
cards.answer: Malarial pigment is a black-brown granular substance derived from haemoglobin degradation; it accumulates in macrophages of the spleen and liver and is a marker of chronic malaria.

tip.tip: Haem (iron) → Oxidized → Haemozoin = Black pigment (like rust)

cards.text: Why is Taenia solium neurocysticercosis epidemiologically important in developing countries?
cards.answer: Neurocysticercosis is the most common helminthic infection of the nervous system and the leading preventable cause of acquired epilepsy in developing countries due to poor sanitation and pork consumption.

tip.tip: Taenia solium → Pigs/poor sanitation → Brain cysts → Seizures (epilepsy leader)

cards.text: How does rosetting contribute to severe malaria pathology?
cards.answer: Rosetting occurs when infected RBCs bind uninfected RBCs, creating large clumps that obstruct cerebral and peripheral microvasculature, exacerbating hypoxia and organ damage.

tip.tip: Rosette = Flower-like cluster; infected RBC clusters block tiny blood vessels
